entries.what_happened: Two manuscripts in the family. (1) 'An infinite finitely presented periodic group' (the companion; build/paper.tex, dated 23 September 2026) constructs a graded, finitely presented unital F₂-algebra R = F₂ ⊕ I, infinite-dimensional, in which every square matrix over I is nilpotent (Theorem thm:algebra). For n ≥ 5 it gives an ordinary finite group presentation of the Steinberg group St_n(R) (Theorem finite-presentation). For n = 12 it claims St₁₂(R) is infinite (its elementary image E₁₂(R) is infinite), that E₁₂(R) is periodic by matrix nilpotence, and that the kernel J₁₂(R) is torsion (Theorem kernel-torsion), so every element of St₁₂(R) has finite order. Its main theorem is that St₁₂(R) is an infinite periodic group with an ordinary finite presentation. (2) 'An infinite finitely presented residually finite 2-group' (build/main.tex, dated 5 October 2026) takes Γ = St₁₂(R) from the companion as given and proves Γ is residually finite, using the finite quotients St₁₂(R/R_≥d). It then passes to G = ker(Γ → St₁₂(F₂)), which has finite index in Γ, and claims G is infinite, ordinarily finitely presented (Reidemeister–Schreier), residually finite, and that every element of G has finite 2-power order, with unbounded orders. Its Theorem thm:main states the existence of an infinite residually finite group with an ordinary finite presentation in which every element has finite 2-power order.
entries.delivers: Gives a negative answer to the yes/no question: there is an infinite finitely presented periodic group. St₁₂(R) from the companion is one, and G from the residual paper is another, which is also residually finite with all element orders 2-powers. 'Periodic' is used in the list's sense: each element has some finite order, with no common exponent. The companion says the order of an element 'may depend on that element', and the residual paper says the orders are unbounded. The presentations are ordinary, with finitely many generators and relators and no variety identities. The companion's introduction states the question in the list's terms ('whether a periodic group with such a presentation must be finite'), and its abstract says the construction answers 'the finitely presented Burnside question negatively'. So the companion's statement of the problem matches the list's. The list places no restriction on characteristic, and the construction uses F₂ only as the ground ring of the algebra R.
entries.remains: Nothing of the yes/no question as stated. Not addressed by either manuscript: finitely presented periodic groups of bounded exponent (the constructed groups have unbounded orders, so they give no information there), and the free Burnside groups B(m,n).
entries.direction: negative answer: exhibits an infinite finitely presented periodic group
entries.object: St₁₂(R) (companion), for a finitely presented F₂-algebra R, and its finite-index subgroup G (residual paper). Both are given by finite presentations: generators g_ij(w) for |w| ≤ 2 over a finite alphabet, with listed commutation, product and algebra-relator families (companion Theorem finite-presentation). The algebra's finite rule table comes from the companion's hierarchy in finite-rules.tex, which I sampled but did not check line by line. The object is explicit as a finite presentation, not an existence-by-counting argument.
entries.conditional_on: The residual paper's residual finiteness and 2-power orders depend on inputs it quotes from the companion: the algebra R and its matrix-nilpotence (companion Theorem 3.7, Proposition ring-input), the word hierarchy used to derive phases (Proposition hierarchy-input), the finite-rank facts for stability (companion Lemma 5.1, Proposition 5.4, Lemma 5.5), and the ordinary finite presentation of Γ (companion Theorem 4.1, and Krstić–McCool Theorem 3). The companion's own claim of an infinite finitely presented periodic group has no unproven hypothesis; it uses the Krstić–McCool method and proves what it uses.
entries.doubts: (a) The residual paper proves none of Γ's infiniteness, presentation or periodicity itself; its new content (residual finiteness, G, 2-power orders) rests on the companion inputs listed above. (b) The residual paper cites companion results by number (Theorem 3.7, Theorem 4.1, Lemma 5.1, Proposition 5.4, Lemma 5.5). The companion labels I read match these by content; I did not confirm the numbering. (c) In proving Proposition finite-quotients, the residual paper says St₁₂(B_d) is perfect without citing the companion lemma that proves it (Lemma fp:perfectness). This is a standard fact but is unproven in the residual text. (d) The companion's periodicity depends on matrices over I being nilpotent, which is proved in cancellation.tex and finite-rules.tex (about 1,650 lines together). Its introduction describes the cancellation mechanism only in prose. I read the statements and portions of those proofs, not all of them.

entries.not_relevant_because: Neither manuscript treats free Burnside groups B(m,n). Their periodic groups have no common exponent: the companion says the order of an element 'may depend on that element', and the residual paper says the orders in its group are unbounded. A group of unbounded exponent is not a quotient of any B(m,n), so these constructions say nothing about whether B(m,n), or B(2,5), is finite.

Köthe's implication concerns rings with no nonzero nil two-sided ideal. The companion's algebra R = F₂ ⊕ I has a nonzero nil two-sided ideal I, which the companion proves is nil (Corollary cor:nil-algebra, item 1), so R falls outside the hypothesis Köthe's question is about. Neither manuscript constructs a ring without a nonzero nil two-sided ideal, and neither addresses one-sided nil ideals in such rings. Their nil results concern Ufnarovskij- and Amitsur-type nilpotence questions and Kurosh-type algebraic finiteness, not the Köthe implication.
